10.01.title: Systems, states and properties
10.01.html:
Thermodynamics is the science of energy and its conversions: fuel into motion in a scooter engine, electricity into heat in a heat pump, falling water into electricity in an Alpine power station. Its first rule of method is to say exactly what you’re analysing. Draw a boundary around it, decide what can cross that boundary, and describe what’s inside by a few numbers. Get this step wrong and every equation afterwards will be wrong too.

Systems

  • A closed system contains a fixed mass. Energy can cross its boundary as heat or work, but matter can’t. Gas in a piston-cylinder is the classic example; the boundary may move.
  • An open system or control volume has mass flowing in and out: a turbine, a pump, a nozzle, a heat exchanger.
  • An isolated system exchanges nothing at all with its surroundings.

Properties and states

A property is any measurable characteristic: pressure p, temperature T, specific volume v=V/m, internal energy u, enthalpy h, entropy s. Intensive properties don’t depend on size (p, T, v); extensive ones do (V, U, m). Dividing an extensive property by mass gives a specific property.

The state is the condition described by the full set of properties. A process takes a system from one state to another.

The state postulate

For a simple compressible substance (no electric, magnetic or surface effects), two independent intensive properties fix the state. Everything else follows from the equation of state and property relations. For an ideal gas,

pv=RT,

so p and T give v. Specifying a third property over-determines the state: it must agree with the first two or the data are inconsistent. (Inside the two-phase region p and T are not independent, 10.06.)

Thermodynamic properties depend only on the state, not on how you got there. Heat and work are not properties: they depend on the path (10.03).

Worked exampleAir as a state object

Air as an ideal gas: R=287 J/(kg K), cp​=1005 J/(kg K).

  1. p=101.325 kPa, T=288.15 K: v=287⋅288.15/101325=0.81618 m³/kg, so ρ=1.2252 kg/m³, the standard sea-level air density.
  2. Specifying T and v instead gives back the same pressure.
  3. Specifying p, T and v=0.9 m³/kg is rejected: pv=91192 J/kg but RT=82699 J/kg.
  4. Specifying only T is rejected: one property doesn’t fix a state.
  5. At 2 MPa and 700 K, with reference 298.15 K: h=1005(700−298.15)=403.86 kJ/kg, and h−u=RΔT, consistent with h=u+pv.

Exercise 1Helium in a balloon

A party balloon holds helium (R=2077 J/(kg K)) at 103 kPa and 25 °C, volume 15 L. Find its specific volume, density and mass.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. v=RT/p=2077⋅298.15/103000=6.012 m³/kg.
  2. ρ=1/v=0.1663 kg/m³.
  3. m=ρV=0.1663⋅0.015=2.49 g.

10.02.title: The ideal gas
10.02.html:
Pump up a scooter tyre and the pump barrel gets warm. Leave the tyre in the Bali sun and its pressure rises. Both follow from the simplest and most used equation in thermodynamics, the ideal-gas law. It holds well for air, nitrogen, helium and combustion gases at ordinary pressures, and you can derive it by imagining molecules as tiny balls bouncing off the walls.

The equation of state

pV=nRu​T=mRT,pv=RT,

with Ru​=8.314 J/(mol K) the universal gas constant and R=Ru​/M the specific gas constant (287 J/(kg K) for air, M=28.97 g/mol). In molecular terms, pV=NkB​T with kB​=1.381×10−23 J/K.

Where it comes from

Consider N molecules of mass m in a cube of side L. A molecule with velocity component vx​ hits the right wall, reverses, and delivers momentum 2mvx​. It returns every 2L/vx​ seconds, so its average force on the wall is mvx2​/L. Summing over all molecules and dividing by the wall area L2:

p=VNm⟨vx2​⟩​=3VNm⟨v2⟩​.

Comparing with pV=NkB​T shows what temperature is: the average translational kinetic energy of the molecules,

21​m⟨v2⟩=23​kB​T.

The rms speed is 3kB​T/m​: about 517 m/s for nitrogen at room temperature, faster than sound.

When is a gas ideal?

The derivation assumed molecules take up no space and don’t attract each other. That’s good when the gas is far from condensing: low pressure, high temperature compared with its critical point. Steam near saturation and refrigerants are not ideal; 10.06 and 10.16 cover them.

Worked examplePressure from collisions

2000 nitrogen molecules in a cube of side 100 nm, with Maxwell-Boltzmann velocities, bounce elastically off the walls for 4000 time steps. The momentum delivered to the walls, divided by wall area and time, is the pressure.

  1. At 300 K (the sample’s kinetic temperature is 293.7 K): simulated 8111.6 Pa against NkB​T/V=8111.0 Pa, ratio 1.0001.
  2. At 200 K and 600 K the ratio is also 1.0001: pressure is proportional to temperature.
  3. The rms speed of N₂ (molecular mass 4.652×10−26 kg) at 300 K is 3kB​T/m​=517 m/s.

Exercise 1A scooter tyre in the sun

A tyre is inflated to 200 kPa gauge (301 kPa absolute) at 25 °C. In the sun it reaches 55 °C at constant volume. What does the gauge read?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. At constant V and m, p∝T: p2​=301⋅328.15/298.15=331.3 kPa absolute.
  2. Gauge: 331.3−101=230 kPa.
  3. Always use absolute temperature and pressure in the gas law.

rms speed (m/s) of helium atoms (m = 6.646×10⁻²⁷ kg) at 300 K. Nearest whole number.
Mass (kg) of air in a 4 × 5 × 3 m room at 101.3 kPa and 20 °C. 2 decimals.
In kinetic theory, temperature measures…

10.03.title: Work and heat
10.03.html:
Squeeze the air in a bicycle pump and you push the handle through a distance against the pressure. That’s work, the same force times distance as in mechanics. In thermodynamics we write it in terms of the gas’s pressure and volume, and it turns out that the amount of work depends on how you squeeze, not just where you start and end.

Boundary work

A gas at pressure p pushes on a piston of area A with force pA. Moving the piston by dx changes the volume by dV=Adx and does work pAdx=pdV. For a slow (quasi-equilibrium) process:

W=∫V1​V2​​pdV.

With the sign convention used here, W>0 when the gas expands and does work on the surroundings, and W<0 for compression. On a p-V diagram, W is the area under the path.

Common processes

  • Isobaric (p constant): W=p(V2​−V1​).
  • Isothermal ideal gas (pV= const): W=p1​V1​ln(V2​/V1​).
  • Polytropic, pVn= const with n=1:
W=1−np2​V2​−p1​V1​​.

n=0 is isobaric, n=1 isothermal, n=k=cp​/cv​ (1.4 for air) is reversible adiabatic, and n→∞ is constant volume (no work).

Heat

Heat Q is energy crossing a boundary because of a temperature difference. Like work, it’s a transfer, not something a system contains. Both depend on the path, which is why we write δQ and δW for small amounts rather than dQ: they aren’t changes of a property.

Worked exampleCompressing 10 L of air to 2 L

Air at 100 kPa and 300 K (11.614 g) compressed from 10 L to 2 L:

  1. Isobaric at 100 kPa: W=100000⋅(−0.008)=−800.0 J.
  2. Isothermal: W=1000ln0.2=−1609.438 J. Numerical integration of pdV gives the same to 10−3 J.
  3. Polytropic n=1.3: p2​=810.3 kPa, T2​=486.2 K, W=−2068.855 J.
  4. Adiabatic n=1.4: p2​=951.8 kPa, T2​=571.1 K, W=−2259.135 J. The steeper the path, the more work it takes, because the gas heats up and pushes back harder.
  5. Two rectangular paths between the same end states take −800 J and −7615 J. Work depends on the path.

Exercise 1A pump stroke

A bicycle pump compresses 0.5 L of air at 100 kPa to 0.1 L so quickly that it’s adiabatic (n=1.4). Find the final pressure and the work input.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. p2​=100⋅51.4=951.8 kPa.
  2. W=(p2​V2​−p1​V1​)/(1−n)=(951.8⋅0.1−100⋅0.5)/(−0.4)=(95.18−50)/(−0.4)=−113.0 J.
  3. You do 113 J of work on the air, and it ends up much hotter. That’s why the pump barrel warms up.

Isothermal work (J) when 2 L of gas at 300 kPa expands to 6 L. 1 decimal.
Isobaric work (kJ) when 1 kg of gas expands from 0.5 to 0.8 m³ at 200 kPa.
Which polytropic exponent describes a constant-volume process?
Heat and work are…
options: Energy transfers that depend on the path

10.04.title: The first law for closed systems
10.04.html:
Energy can’t be created or destroyed, only converted. In mechanics that meant kinetic plus potential energy stays constant without friction. Thermodynamics extends the bookkeeping to heat and internal energy, the energy of the molecules' random motion. It’s the first law, and every energy calculation you’ll ever do, from a pressure cooker to a power station, is an application of it.

The first law

For a closed system going from state 1 to state 2:

Q−W=ΔU(+ΔKE+ΔPE),

with Q the heat added to the system and W the work done by it. In differential form, δQ−δW=dU.

U is a property: its change depends only on the end states. Q and W depend on the path, but their difference doesn’t. Over a full cycle the system returns to its start, ΔU=0, so

∮δQ=∮δW:

a cycle’s net work equals its net heat input.

Internal energy and enthalpy of ideal gases

For an ideal gas, u depends only on temperature: du=cv​dT. The enthalpy h=u+pv is also a function of T only, dh=cp​dT, with cp​−cv​=R. For air near room temperature cv​=718 and cp​=1005 J/(kg K).

At constant pressure, heat added equals the change in enthalpy: Q=ΔU+pΔV=ΔH. That’s why enthalpy appears whenever pressure is held fixed, or whenever fluid flows (10.05).

Solving problems

  1. Choose the system and draw the boundary.
  2. Identify the processes and what’s fixed in each (p, V, T, or adiabatic).
  3. Find the end states from the equation of state.
  4. Compute W along each path and ΔU from the end states.
  5. Get Q from the first law, and check that the residual Q−W−ΔU is zero.

Worked exampleHeating air under a piston with stops

2 L of air at 150 kPa and 300 K (3.4843 g) sits under a free piston. It’s heated at constant pressure to 500 K, when the piston reaches stops, then heated at constant volume to 700 K.

  1. Constant pressure: V2​=2⋅500/300=3.333 L. W=150000⋅0.001333=200.0 J. ΔU=0.0034843⋅718⋅200=500.3 J. Q=700.3 J.
  2. Constant volume: W=0, ΔU=Q=500.3 J. Final pressure 210.0 kPa.
  3. Totals: Q=1200.7 J, W=200.0 J, ΔU=1000.7 J =mcv​(700−300). The residual is zero in every step.
  4. An Otto-like cycle (adiabatic compression to 0.5 L, constant-volume heating by 400 K, adiabatic expansion, constant-volume cooling): net Q = net W = 425.73 J and ΔU=0 around the cycle.

Exercise 1A rigid tank

A rigid 50 L tank holds air at 100 kPa and 20 °C. A 200 W heater runs for 2 minutes and the tank loses 4 kJ of heat to the room meanwhile. Find the final temperature and pressure.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. m=pV/(RT)=100000⋅0.05/(287⋅293.15)=0.05943 kg.
  2. Net heat: 200⋅120−4000=20000 J. Rigid tank, no boundary work. The electric heater’s input counts as electrical work done on the system, W=−24 kJ, with Q=−4 kJ. Either way ΔU=20 kJ.
  3. ΔT=20000/(0.05943⋅718)=468.7 K, so T2​=761.8 K.
  4. p2​=100⋅761.8/293.15=259.9 kPa.

10.05.title: The first law for open systems
10.05.html:
Most energy machines have fluid flowing through them: air through a jet engine, steam through a turbine, water through a pump, refrigerant through a heat pump. We can’t follow a fixed lump of mass through them easily, so we draw a fixed control volume around the machine and keep account of energy carried in and out by the flow. In steady operation the result is one of the most useful equations in engineering.

Flow work and enthalpy

Pushing fluid into a control volume takes work: a slug of volume V pushed in against pressure p needs pV, or pv per kilogram. This flow work always accompanies the internal energy u carried in, so the natural combination is the enthalpy, h=u+pv.

The steady-flow energy equation

For one inlet (1) and one outlet (2) with mass flow m˙, steady operation:

Q˙​−W˙=m˙[(h2​−h1​)+2V22​−V12​​+g(z2​−z1​)].

W˙ is shaft power out; flow work is already inside h.

Typical devices

  • Nozzle: no work, nearly adiabatic. The enthalpy drop becomes kinetic energy: V2​=V12​+2(h1​−h2​)​.
  • Turbine: adiabatic, kinetic energy changes small. W˙=m˙(h1​−h2​).
  • Compressor or pump: the same with work in. For a pump with liquid, h2​−h1​≈vΔp.
  • Throttle valve: no work, no heat, so h2​=h1​. An ideal gas leaves at the same temperature; a real fluid can cool sharply (10.15).
  • Heat exchanger: no work; heat lost by one stream equals heat gained by the other.

Orders of magnitude: 1 K of temperature in water is 4186 J/kg; 1 m of height is 9.81 J/kg; a speed of 45 m/s is 1000 J/kg. Kinetic and potential terms matter only in nozzles, diffusers and hydropower (10.07).

For an ideal gas flowing through a reversible adiabatic device, T2​/T1​=(p2​/p1​)(k−1)/k (10.10 covers real devices).

Worked exampleNozzle, turbine and compressor

Air with cp​=1005 J/(kg K), k=1.4.

  1. Nozzle: 500 K, 300 kPa, 30 m/s in, expanding isentropically to 100 kPa. T2​=500⋅(1/3)0.2857=365.36 K, so V2​=302+2⋅1005⋅134.64​=521.1 m/s. The energy residual is zero.
  2. Turbine: 2 kg/s from 1200 K and 1 MPa to 100 kPa. Exit 621.7 K, power 1162.3 kW.
  3. Compressor: 2 kg/s from 300 K and 100 kPa to 1 MPa. Exit 579.0 K, power absorbed 560.8 kW.
  4. Together they deliver 601.5 kW: the heart of a gas turbine (10.13).
  5. Throttle: h2​=h1​ gives zero power residual, and for an ideal gas no temperature change.

Exercise 1A water pump

A pump lifts 20 kg/s of water from 100 kPa to 1.5 MPa (v=0.001 m³/kg). Neglecting heat loss and velocity changes, what power does it need if it’s ideal? What temperature rise would friction cause if the pump were only 70 % efficient?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Ideal: W˙=m˙vΔp=20⋅0.001⋅1.4×106=28.0 kW.
  2. Actual: 28.0/0.7=40.0 kW. The extra 12.0 kW is dissipated into the water.
  3. ΔT=12000/(20⋅4186)=0.14 K. Pump losses barely warm the water, so measuring that rise needs very precise thermometers.

Ideal pump power (kW) for 20 kg/s of water raised by 1.4 MPa.
Isentropic exit temperature (K) of air expanded from 1000 K by a pressure ratio of 8. 1 decimal.
Across a throttle valve…

10.06.title: Pure substances and phase change
10.06.html:
Put a pan of water on the stove. It warms until it reaches 100 °C, then stays at 100 °C for a long time while it boils. All that energy goes into turning liquid into vapour, not into raising the temperature. Up a mountain the water boils at a lower temperature; in a pressure cooker at a higher one. Steam is far from an ideal gas, so engineers use property tables, and these days property libraries, to analyse boilers, turbines and heat pumps.

Phases and saturation

At a given pressure, liquid water boils at one saturation temperature Tsat​(p); equivalently each temperature has a saturation pressure. Between the saturated liquid state (f) and the saturated vapour state (g), the substance is a wet mixture whose temperature and pressure stay fixed while it boils. Beyond g it’s superheated vapour; below f, compressed liquid.

In the two-phase region p and T aren’t independent, so they can’t fix the state together. The quality x, the mass fraction of vapour, is the second property:

v=vf​+x(vg​−vf​),h=hf​+xhfg​,s=sf​+x(sg​−sf​).

Solving for x from any one known property gives the rest.

Reading tables in code

A saturation table lists psat​, vf​, vg​, hf​, hg​, sf​, sg​ at chosen temperatures. Between rows, interpolate. Linear interpolation is fine for h and s, but psat​ and vg​ change exponentially with temperature (the Clausius-Clapeyron relation, lnp≈A−B/T). Interpolating lnp against 1/T is far more accurate.

The latent heat hfg​ falls as temperature rises and reaches zero at the critical point (374 °C, 22.06 MPa), where liquid and vapour become indistinguishable.

Worked exampleUsing the table

Saturation table for water from 10 to 300 °C (IAPWS-95 values).

  1. The interpolation function reproduces every tabulated row exactly.
  2. Between rows, compared with IAPWS-95: at 45 °C, psat​=9.5895 kPa (true 9.595), hf​=188.44 kJ/kg (188.435), vg​=15.262 m³/kg (15.252). At 150 °C: 475.78 kPa (476.17) and hf​=632.32 (632.18).
  3. Wet steam at 100 °C with x=0.9: v=1.5047 m³/kg, h=419.17+0.9⋅2256.40=2449.93 kJ/kg, s=6.7494 kJ/(kg K).
  4. Recovering the quality from h gives 0.9 exactly.

Exercise 1A rigid tank of wet steam

A rigid 0.5 m³ tank contains 2 kg of water at 120 °C. What’s the quality, and how much is vapour by mass and by volume?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. v=0.5/2=0.25 m³/kg. At 120 °C, vf​=0.001060 and vg​=0.8912 m³/kg, so it’s a wet mixture.
  2. x=(0.25−0.00106)/(0.8912−0.00106)=0.2797.
  3. Vapour mass: 0.2797⋅2=0.559 kg, occupying 0.559⋅0.8912=0.4985 m³, so 99.7 % of the volume. The liquid is only 1.44 kg in about 1.5 litres.

Latent heat (kJ/kg) at 200 °C from the table (h_f = 852.27, h_g = 2792.01). 2 decimals.

10.07.title: Pumped-storage hydropower
10.07.html:
Solar panels produce most at midday in summer; demand peaks on winter evenings. Storing electricity at grid scale is hard, and over 90 % of the world’s grid storage is one old idea: pump water uphill when power is cheap, let it run back through a turbine when power is scarce. Switzerland, with lakes hundreds of metres above each other, has some of the largest schemes in Europe. The thermodynamics is the first law with gravitational potential energy.

Energy stored

Lifting a volume V of water through a head h stores

E=ρghV.

It’s linear in both head and volume. One kilowatt-hour, 3.6×106 J, needs 3.6×106/(ρgh) m³ of water: 1.22 m³ falling 300 m, or 367 m³ falling 1 m. That’s why pumped storage needs mountains. A flat-land scheme would need a lake the size of a city.

Power is the flow rate times the head: P=ηρgQh, so a 900 MW plant at 300 m head moves about 340 m³ of water every second.

Round-trip efficiency

Every conversion loses something.

  • Generating: turbine (about 92 %), generator (98 %), and penstock friction, which takes a head hf​ off the available head.
  • Pumping: pump (about 91 %), motor (98 %), and the pump must deliver h+hf​.

Friction head follows Darcy-Weisbach, hf​=fDL​2gV2​, so penstocks are built several metres in diameter to keep the speed low. Multiplying the efficiencies gives the round trip, typically 75–82 %. About a fifth of the electricity is lost, but storing it is worth far more when the price difference between night and peak, or summer and winter, is large enough.

Worked exampleAn Alpine plant

Assumed round numbers loosely modelled on a large Alpine scheme: 25 million m³ upper reservoir, 300 m mean head, 900 MW, two penstocks 1.4 km long and 7 m in diameter.

  1. Stored energy: 1000⋅9.81⋅300⋅25×106=7.358×1013 J =20.44 GWh.
  2. Flow at full power: Q=P/(ρgh⋅0.90)=340 m³/s, 170 m³/s per penstock, about 4.4 m/s.
  3. Friction head: 2.38 m, only 0.79 % of the head.
  4. Generating efficiency 0.92⋅0.98⋅(1−0.0079)=0.894; pumping 0.91⋅0.98/(1+0.0079)=0.885; round trip 0.791.
  5. It returns 18.28 GWh for 23.10 GWh pumped in: 20.3 hours at full power.

Exercise 1Is it worth it?

A plant buys electricity at 40 CHF/MWh at night and sells at 120 CHF/MWh at the evening peak, with a round-trip efficiency of 0.79. What’s the margin per MWh sold, and what’s the minimum price ratio that breaks even? Also find the energy stored in a smaller reservoir of 2 million m³ at 500 m head.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Each MWh sold needs 1/0.79=1.266 MWh bought, costing 40/0.79=50.63 CHF.
  2. Margin: 120−50.63=69.37 CHF per MWh, before maintenance and grid fees.
  3. Break-even when sell/buy price =1/0.79=1.266.
  4. Smaller reservoir: 1000⋅9.81⋅500⋅2×106=9.81×1012 J =2.725 GWh. The higher head partly makes up for the much smaller volume.

quiz.q: Energy (GWh) stored by 2 million m³ at 500 m head. 3 decimals.
Volume of water (m³) falling 300 m that stores 1 kWh. 3 decimals.
Round trip with generating 0.894 and pumping 0.885. 3 decimals.
Doubling the head with the same volume does what to the stored energy?
Why are penstocks several metres in diameter?

10.08.title: The second law and the Carnot limit
10.08.html:
The first law says energy is conserved. It doesn’t say which way things go. A hot coffee cools in a cold room; it never spontaneously gets hotter. A car’s engine turns at most about 40 % of its fuel energy into work, not because engineers are careless but because nature sets a ceiling. The second law of thermodynamics is that ceiling, and the Carnot efficiency puts a number on it.

Two statements

  • Kelvin-Planck: no cyclic device can take heat from a single reservoir and turn it all into work. Every heat engine must reject some heat to a colder sink.
  • Clausius: heat can’t flow from cold to hot on its own. A refrigerator needs work input.

The two are equivalent: a device violating one can be combined with an ordinary engine or fridge to violate the other.

The Carnot efficiency

A reversible engine between a hot reservoir at Th​ and a cold one at Tc​ (in kelvin) has efficiency

ηCarnot​=1−Th​Tc​​.

No engine working between the same two reservoirs can do better, and all reversible ones do exactly this well. In general, for any cycle the Clausius inequality holds:

∮TδQ​≤0,

with equality only for reversible cycles. On a T-s diagram a reversible cycle’s heat input is the area under its top, and its net work the enclosed area. The Carnot cycle is a rectangle, the shape that uses the temperature limits best. Any other shape between the same limits takes in heat below Th​ or rejects it above Tc​, and does worse.

The practical lesson is: raise Th​ (hotter combustion, superheated steam, better turbine blade alloys) and lower Tc​ (cold river water, cooling towers). A 150 °C geothermal source can never exceed 29.5 % however clever the machine.

Worked exampleNo shape beats the rectangle

  1. Between 300 K and 900 K the Carnot limit is 1−300/900=0.6667.
  2. A rectangle on the T-s diagram reproduces it to machine precision.
  3. 20 000 random reversible cycles drawn inside the same band: the best manages 0.5330, and every one stays below the Carnot limit for its own temperature extremes.
  4. Real limits: a coal plant with 565 °C steam and a 25 °C river, 64.4 % (real plants reach about 45 %); an engine with 2300 K peak gas and 300 K air, 87.0 %; geothermal at 150 °C, 29.5 %.

Exercise 1Check an inventor’s claim

An inventor says her engine takes 1000 kJ from a reservoir at 500 K, delivers 450 kJ of work and rejects 550 kJ to the surroundings at 300 K. Is it possible? Check both the efficiency and the Clausius inequality.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. The first law is satisfied: 1000=450+550.
  2. Claimed efficiency 450/1000=0.45; Carnot limit 1−300/500=0.40. Impossible.
  3. Clausius: ∮δQ/T=1000/500−550/300=2.000−1.833=+0.167 kJ/K, which is greater than zero, so the cycle violates the second law.
  4. To be possible it would need to reject at least 1000⋅300/500=600 kJ.

quiz.q: Carnot efficiency between 25 °C and 565 °C. 4 decimals.
Clausius integral (kJ/K) for the inventor’s engine. 4 decimals.
Minimum heat (kJ) rejected at 300 K for 1000 kJ taken at 500 K.
Which statement says no engine can turn all the heat from one reservoir into work?
On a T-s diagram, which cycle uses fixed temperature limits best?

10.09.title: Entropy
10.09.html:
Mix hot and cold water in a shower and you get warm water. Energy is perfectly conserved, yet something has been lost: you can’t unmix them, and you’ve thrown away the chance to run an engine between the hot and cold supplies. Entropy is the property that measures that loss. It increases in every real process and stays constant only in ideal reversible ones.

Definition

For a reversible process, entropy changes by

dS=TδQrev​​.

Entropy is a property: its change between two states is the same whatever the process, reversible or not. To calculate it, invent any convenient reversible path. For an incompressible liquid or solid with specific heat c,

Δs=clnT1​T2​​.

Entropy generation

For a real process the balance gains a generation term that can’t be negative:

ΔSsystem​=∫Tb​δQ​+Sgen​,Sgen​≥0,

where Tb​ is the temperature at the boundary where the heat crosses. For a steady-flow device, ∑m˙out​sout​−∑m˙in​sin​=∑Q˙​/Tb​+S˙gen​.

Sources of generation: heat transfer across a finite temperature difference, friction, mixing, unrestrained expansion, electrical resistance. Engineering for efficiency is largely hunting these down.

Mixing two streams

In an insulated mixer, the energy balance gives the exit temperature T3​=(m˙1​T1​+m˙2​T2​)/(m˙1​+m˙2​). The hot stream loses entropy, the cold one gains more than that, and

S˙gen​=m˙1​clnT1​T3​​+m˙2​clnT2​T3​​≥0,

zero only when T1​=T2​. Because ln is concave, the weighted log of the mean temperature is always larger than the weighted mean of the logs.

Worked exampleA shower

0.08 kg/s of hot water at 60 °C mixes with 0.04 kg/s of cold at 15 °C; c=4.186 kJ/(kg K).

  1. Exit temperature: (0.08⋅333.15+0.04⋅288.15)/0.12=318.15 K =45.00 °C.
  2. Hot stream: 0.08⋅4.186ln(318.15/333.15)=−0.015428 kW/K. Cold: 0.04⋅4.186ln(318.15/288.15)=+0.016584 kW/K.
  3. S˙gen​=1.1557 W/K. With surroundings at T0​=288.15 K the lost work potential is T0​S˙gen​=333.01 W.
  4. 100 000 random mixings never give negative generation.
  5. Heating 1 kg of water from 15 to 60 °C changes its entropy by 0.60744 kJ/K whatever the process. From a 60 °C reservoir, the reservoir loses 4.186⋅45/333.15, so 0.04202 kJ/K is generated.

Exercise 1An insulated bucket

Pour 1 kg of water at 80 °C into 2 kg at 20 °C in an insulated bucket. Find the final temperature, the entropy generated and the lost work with surroundings at 20 °C.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. T3​=(353.15+2⋅293.15)/3=313.15 K =40 °C.
  2. Hot: 4.186ln(313.15/353.15)=−0.50320 kJ/K. Cold: 2⋅4.186ln(313.15/293.15)=+0.55253 kJ/K.
  3. Sgen​=0.04933 kJ/K, positive as it must be.
  4. Lost work T0​Sgen​=293.15⋅0.04933=14.46 kJ: an ideal engine running between the two buckets could have produced that before they reached 40 °C.
